newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook-West gives unexpected boost.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook-West gives unexpected boost.

text.p: The unexpected shutdown of three secondary processing units in Europe has given Asian light and middle distillate prices an unexpected boost despite poor regional fundamentals, traders said on Monday.
The shutdown of the catalytic converters came at a time of strong European demand for gasoline and diesel at the peak of the driving season.
Prices were also lifted sharply with more gains expected in Europe later this week with the effects rippling into Asia, traders said.
The impact was already seen in the Asian gas oil market where, despite an extremely low award by India for September-arrival cargoes, prices have in fact risen.
"The price increase is unexpected," one trader said. "It is due to the shutdown of the three cat-cracker units in Europe which have pushed the numbers up."

Two catalytic converters--one at the BP/Texaco Nerefco refinery in Rotterdam and one at the BP/Mobil Coryton refinery in the U.K.--were closed on Friday due to technical problems. These shutdowns will remove 115,000 barrels per day (bpd) of capacity until the middle of next week.
In addition, Shell confirmed on Friday that the cat-cracker at its Pernis refinery has closed for an unscheduled stoppage in August followed by a scheduled maintenance of two months.

The market's resilience was first tested by news that Indian Oil Corp (IOC) had bought a meagre 90,000 tonnes of high-speed diesel in two cargoes for September delivery, well below even the most conservative estimate of 200,000 tonnes.

"This is a low volume time of the year," one trader said. "But the fact that India took the much lower volume is surprising. I think they are trying to talk down the market in anticipation of some term talks."

The two 45,000-tonne cargoes are for delivery to Madras or Haldia on the Indian east coast at a premium of 47 cents per barrel to Singapore spot quotes, on a cost-and-freight basis. The winners were Shell and Cargill, traders said.
IOC took 165,000 tonnes of diesel in August and 855,000 tonnes in July.
Traders said although it was highly unlikely for Singapore barrels to head West, but firmer European prices will definitely attract any incremental cargoes available from the Middle East.
But some traders said gas oil supplies in the Middle East would be tight until at least mid-August.

In addition to shutdowns in the West, regional maintenance of crude units in Indonesia, South Korea and Japan, as well as cuts in refining rates in Singapore, are likely to curb excess supplies, they said.
The shutdown of Shell Singapore's 11,000 tonne-per-day (82,000-bpd) thermal gas oil unit in August for 21-days will also reduce supplies slightly, traders said.
They said the jet fuel market is also holding its own and is poised to for a new rally as players begin building stocks ahead of the winter.

But they said the large rise in middle distillate stocks in several storage terminals across the region--China, Guam, Singapore and the Middle East--might limit any large price hikes this winter compared to previous years.

Last winter, jet fuel and gas oil prices soared to trade at around $34.00 per barrel on a free-on-board (fob) Singapore basis, giving many storage players a decent profit, even though it was not as big as in 1995 amid a severe winter.
The prompt weakness has led to a steep contango on swaps jet fuel prices, where the present value is much cheaper than the forward price.
The contango, which exceeds $4.00 per barrel, sufficiently pays for the four or five months that the companies have to keep the oil products in storage, they said.
It costs about 50 cents to store one barrel of middle distillate for a month in most of the regional independent storage terminals, traders said
The current price of jet-kerosene fuel is around $22.60 per barrel, compared to $26.50 in the fourth quarter and $27.20 in the first quarter of 1998, brokers said.
Gasoline prices are also set to rise on the back of the European shutdowns, traders said.
Prices in Asia have fallen over the past week due to poor regional demand unlike in the Europe where prices have risen by $25.00 over the past two weeks.
Traders said the market here might be dragged up as the it enters the last leg of the peak northern hemisphere summer demand.
The latest numbers into Taiwan's Chinese Petroleum Corp's (CPC) tender to purchase September-arrival cargoes attest to the general bullish sentiment, they said.

Taiwan last week cancelled its bi-monthly tender to buy reformate for September 1-15 because of high offers and is expected to re-issue a new tender later on Monday in the hope of securing lower offers.
But some traders said it would be difficult for CPC to secure lower offers.
CPC was only prepared to accept offers of less than $25.00 per barrel and considered the lowest offer of around $25.30 too high.
